title: Gig Worker Taxes Without the Panic: What to Set Aside (US)
description: Gig worker taxes explained for US delivery and rideshare drivers: how much to set aside from every payout, quarterly due dates and deductions.

cover.alt: An insulated delivery bag, a phone showing a map and a jar of coins

keywords: gig worker taxes doordash taxes how much to set aside for taxes 1099 self employment tax quarterly estimated taxes mileage deduction
takeaways: Move about 25% of every payout into a separate tax account the day it lands, or 30% if you have another job.
Self-employment tax applies once net earnings reach $400 a year, and the IRS expects payments during the year.
Log your miles as you go. In 2026 the IRS rate is 72.5 cents a mile to June 30 and 76 cents from July 1.
body:
If you deliver food, drive passengers, or shop for grocery orders through an app in the United States, this guide is for you. It covers US federal taxes only, written for someone earning around $300 a week from DoorDash or a similar app alongside classes or another job. Your state may have its own income tax on top. The whole approach fits in one sentence: every time a payout lands, move a fixed percentage into a separate account that same day, then send it to the IRS on four set dates during the year. Everything below explains which percentage to use, what to do in your very first quarter when there is no last-year tax bill to copy, and how a few minutes of weekly tracking makes the final bill smaller. ## Why nobody takes tax out of your pay A regular job quietly handles your taxes for you: your employer holds back income tax, Social Security, and Medicare from every paycheck before you see the money. Gig apps skip all of that. The full payout arrives, and the tax side becomes your job. That is because the IRS treats most app workers as self-employed, not as employees of the app, which means two separate taxes come out of what you earn: - Income tax, figured on your profit for the year, the same basic tax everyone pays. - Self-employment tax, which covers Social Security and Medicare. An employee pays 7.65% of wages and the employer pays another 7.65%. Working for yourself, you pay the full 15.3%: 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. Two more ground rules matter early. Once your net earnings from self-employment reach $400 in a year, you have to file a tax return, even if gig work is a small side thing. And the IRS collects tax on a pay as you go basis, so it expects payments during the year, not one big payment next spring. New to earning this way? [Side hustles for students](/blog/side-hustles-for-students-zero-investment/) covers choosing the work and getting started; this guide picks up when the first payout lands. ## The one habit: set aside a percentage of every payout Pick a percentage, and move that share of every single payout into a separate savings account on the day the money arrives. For most beginners, 25% of each payout is a good starting point. A percentage beats a fixed dollar amount because gig income refuses to sit still. It grows in a busy week and shrinks in a slow one, so you never promise the tax pot money you did not earn. The transfer takes ten seconds, and doing it the same day matters: money that sits in a spending account for a week tends to get spent. If you already budget around income that changes monthly, this will feel familiar. Read next: [How to Budget With Irregular Income](/blog/budget-with-irregular-income/). The tax account is the strictest version of that idea, since its deadlines are not flexible. One reassurance: the IRS is fine with money moving toward your bill more often than four times a year; you may even pay weekly or monthly if you prefer. ### Why 25% is a sensible number That 15.3% rate is charged on 92.35% of your profit, so it lands closer to 14 cents per dollar of profit, and you can deduct half the tax itself when figuring income tax. Income tax only applies to profit left after expenses and the standard deduction, which is why many part-time drivers owe little or no federal income tax on top. Now notice the quiet advantage. You set aside 25% of the payout, but taxes are figured on profit, and profit is smaller than the payout once mileage and other costs come off. That gap is your cushion. If you also have a second job, run very low expenses, or live in a state with an income tax, push the habit to 30%. And if money is left over after you file, that is a good problem: move it into your emergency savings and start the new year clean. Read next: [How to Build an Emergency Fund on a Low Income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/). ### Give the money its own account Open a second savings account used for nothing else, and name it something blunt like Tax Pot. Money meant for the IRS that sits in your everyday account tends to turn into takeout by week three. If it earns a little interest while it waits, that is a bonus. Read next: [What Is a High-Yield Savings Account?](/blog/high-yield-savings-account/). ## A worked example on $300 a week The figures below are an illustration with made-up numbers, not a promise about your bill. Say a student delivers on weekends and some evenings, averages $300 a week in payouts, and drives about 1,200 business miles across a three-month fall stretch. | Payouts over 13 weeks (13 x $300) | $3,900 | |--------------------------------------------------|-------------| | Moved to the tax account at 25% | $975 | | Business miles (1,200 miles x 76 cents) | $912 | | Other work costs: phone share, bags, phone mount | $88 | | Total work costs | $1,000 | | Profit ($3,900 minus $1,000) | $2,900 | | Self-employment tax (15.3% of 92.35% of profit) | About $410 | If gig work were this student's only income all year, yearly profit would be about $11,600, below the standard deduction, so federal income tax would be zero and the quarterly bill roughly that $410 of self-employment tax. The account holds $975 by payment day, leaving about $565 of cushion for a campus job, a busier season, or state tax to eat into. ## Your first quarter, when there is no last-year bill to copy Most tax guides tell you to take last year's total tax, divide it by four, and pay that each quarter. That works fine for established freelancers. It is useless if last year you had no gig income at all, and first-year gig workers are usually the ones reading guides like this. Build your estimate from this year instead. After three or four payouts you know your weekly average, and that is enough to start. Pay based on what you actually earned in each period, then adjust the next payment as real numbers come in. The IRS expects estimates to be revised this way: Form 1040-ES, the estimated tax form, has a worksheet for your amount, and redoing it each quarter is normal, not suspicious. There is also a genuine break for beginners. The IRS says you do not have to pay estimated tax for a year if you owed no tax the year before, you were a US citizen or resident alien for that whole year, and that year covered 12 months. Plenty of students fit that description. Treat it as breathing room, not a free pass: the tax on this year's income is still due when you file, so keep moving 25% aside from the first payout. Timing trips people up, so be clear on this: you only pay on income already earned. Start delivering in October and your first payment covers what you earned from September 1 to December 31, due the following January 15. The months before you started owe nothing. ## The four payment dates These payments are what people mean by quarterly taxes for gig workers, although the four periods are not equal, and the second is strangely short. The IRS splits the year like this: | Income earned Jan 1 to Mar 31 | Due April 15 | |-------------------------------|---------------------------------| | Income earned Apr 1 to May 31 | Due June 15 | | Income earned Jun 1 to Aug 31 | Due September 15 | | Income earned Sep 1 to Dec 31 | Due January 15 of the next year | If a due date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, it moves to the next business day. For earnings from the fall of 2026, the date to circle is January 15, 2027. Paying online is quickest, through IRS Direct Pay or your IRS online account, though you can also mail a check with a Form 1040-ES voucher. Save the confirmation either way: every payment is credited against your final bill when you file. ## Track miles and expenses as you go Expenses are the reason 25% of the payout ends up being enough. Every work cost lowers your profit, and lower profit shrinks both taxes. The catch is that records need to be made at the time. A mileage total invented from memory in April will not hold up, and it will probably be too low anyway. For drivers, mileage is the deduction that matters most. Using the IRS standard mileage rate, business driving in 2026 is worth 72.5 cents per mile from January 1 to June 30, and 76 cents per mile from July 1 to December 31. The rate stands in for gas, wear, and repairs, so you do not track those separately when you use it. Log the date, the miles, and what the driving was for, in a glove box notebook or an app, as long as the entry happens the same day. Keep simple records of other work costs too: the business share of your phone bill, insulated bags, a phone mount, tolls and parking paid while working. Selling goods online instead of driving? Your list is supplies, packaging, and postage. Small numbers, recorded weekly, beat a shoebox of receipts in January. For one simple place to record payouts, miles, and weekly set-asides, our free spreadsheet was made for exactly that job.

Download the free Gig Income and Tax Tracker (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The Quarters tab of the gig income tracker, totalling payouts, set-asides, costs and a rough self-employment tax for each IRS period](/assets/img/posts/gig-income-tax-tracker-preview-1280x542.webp) ## What lands in your mailbox in January Platforms report what they paid you, and you should receive copies of any forms by January 31. Depending on the app, that might be a Form 1099-K, a Form 1099-NEC, or a Form 1099-MISC. First time filing a return at all? [How to file taxes for the first time](/blog/file-taxes-first-time/) walks through the whole process. Do not treat a missing form as missing income. The thresholds for when a platform must send these forms have changed several times in recent years, which is why older articles argue about the numbers. The rule underneath has not moved: the IRS says all gig income is taxable and belongs on your return, whether reported on a form, paid in cash, or held in an app, full time or side gig. At filing time, gig income and expenses go on Schedule C, and self-employment tax is worked out on Schedule SE. Keep your four payment confirmations with the forms, since those payments are credited against the final total. ## If you are already behind Reading this in your third quarter with nothing set aside? Send something now anyway. The penalty for paying too little is worked out period by period and grows while an amount stays unpaid, so a partial payment today costs less than a perfect one next month. Then restart the 25% habit with your next payout. For scale, most taxpayers avoid the penalty if what they still owe after withholding and credits is under $1,000, or if they paid at least 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's, whichever is smaller. One rough quarter is a setback, not a disaster. ## Frequently asked questions ### How much should I set aside from each payout? Start with 25% of every payout, moved to a separate account the day you are paid. Use 30% if another job pushes your income up, you have few expenses to deduct, or your state taxes income. ### Do I owe tax if I only made a few hundred dollars? Once net self-employment earnings reach $400 in a year, you must file a return and self-employment tax applies. Below that, the tax does not apply, though filing can still be worthwhile, for example to claim back tax withheld from a regular job. ### What if no app sends me a 1099? Report it anyway. Your duty to report does not depend on a form arriving, and the payout history inside the app is your backup record. ### Can I skip the quarterly payments and just pay in April? You can pay then, but the IRS can charge an underpayment penalty for each missed period, even if the full amount arrives with your return. Quarterly payments spread the cost and skip that penalty. ### I also have a part-time job. Does that change anything? Yes, and it can make life simpler. Ask your employer to withhold extra tax from your wages by filing a new Form W-4. Withholding counts toward your bill just like estimated payments, and some students use it to cover gig tax and skip quarterly payments altogether. ### What about state taxes? Many states tax gig income too, with their own forms and payment dates. Check your state tax agency's website early in the year, and consider setting aside a few extra percent as a buffer. A quick note: this article is general information about US federal taxes, not tax or financial advice for your situation. Rules, rates, and dates change, and your state, filing status, and other income all affect the real numbers. Confirm current details on IRS.gov, or talk with a qualified tax professional before you file. ## Sources - [IRS, Manage Taxes for Your Gig Work](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/manage-taxes-for-your-gig-work) - [IRS, Estimated Taxes](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/estimated-taxes) - [IRS, Pay As You Go: A Guide to Withholding, Estimated Taxes and Ways to Avoid the Estimated Tax Penalty](https://www.irs.gov/payments/pay-as-you-go-so-you-wont-owe-a-guide-to-withholding-estimated-taxes-and-ways-to-avoid-the-estimated-tax-penalty) - [IRS, Standard Mileage Rates](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/standard-mileage-rates)
